t: Alert Using Same Key-Card Three or More Times in a One Hour Period: Sorted Triple Check
o:
## Understanding the problem

Each (name, "HH:MM") pair is one key-card use. A worker is flagged if some three of their uses fit inside a span of at most 60 minutes, boundaries included: 10:00-11:00 counts (exactly 60 apart), while 22:51-23:52 does not (61 apart). Everything happens within a single day, so there is no midnight wraparound. Report flagged names alphabetically.

Example 1: daniel's uses at 10:00, 10:40, 11:00 span exactly 60 minutes - flagged. Luis's four uses sit hours apart - safe.

Example 2: alice's uses (12:01, 12:00, 18:00) never put three within an hour; bob's 21:00, 21:20, 21:30 do - answer ["bob"]. Note alice's events arrive out of order, so per-person sorting is mandatory before any window logic.

With up to 100000 events, quadratic checks per worker can explode if one worker dominates the input; sorting once and testing consecutive triples keeps things linear after the sort.
k: Convert HH:MM to absolute minutes immediately so window checks become integer subtractions.
After sorting, if any three uses fit in an hour, some consecutive triple does; checking t[i+2] - t[i] <= 60 suffices.
The boundary is inclusive: exactly 60 minutes between first and third use still triggers the alert.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort, Then Scan All Hour Windows
a.i: Group events by worker, sort each list, and for every starting use count how many uses fall within the following 60 minutes by walking forward until the span breaks. Clear and obviously correct; the early break on span violation keeps typical inputs fast even though the worst case is quadratic per worker.
s: For each start index i, advance j while ts[j] - ts[i] <= 60 and count uses.
If any window reaches 3, flag that worker once and stop scanning them.
Return flagged names in sorted order.
a.t: O(n log n + sum k^2) - sorting plus pairwise hourly scans per worker with k uses.

a.i: Key observation: in a sorted list, if any three uses fit inside an hour, then in particular the triple starting at that window's first index does. So a single linear pass comparing ts[i+2] - ts[i] <= 60 replaces all pairwise scans and is enough for a flag.
s: Bucket minute-stamps by name and sort each bucket.
For i from 0 to k-3, check whether ts[i+2] - ts[i] <= 60.
Flag the worker on the first hit and break out.
a.t: O(n log n) - sorting each worker's stamps dominates; the scan is linear.

w:
State the consecutive-triple lemma before coding Approach 2 - it is the whole solution - and keep Approach 1 as your correctness baseline.

**Pitfalls.** Treating a 61-minute spread as inside the window; skipping the per-person sort when input interleaves workers; emitting duplicate names; parsing "HH:MM" without splitting off the colon.

**Follow-ups.** Alerts across midnight (wraparound windows over minutes mod 1440); generalized thresholds (k uses in m minutes); streaming detection with bounded memory per worker.
